title: Biodegradable pectin films incorporating purple sweet potato anthocyanins for real-time shrimp freshness monitoring
abstract: Abstract This study aimed to develop biodegradable films using pectin extracted from orange peel residues, purple sweet potato extract, and glycerol, with potential application for monitoring shrimp freshness. The physical, barrier, mechanical, bioactive, antioxidant, morphological, structural, and thermal properties of the developed material were evaluated, as well as its viability as a freshness indicator for shrimp. The extracted pectin showed a high yield (45.44%), equivalent weight (1807.76 g), and methoxyl content (79.26%), indicating the quality of the obtained biopolymer. Films containing anthocyanin extract from purple sweet potato (FE) exhibited a predictable and sensitive color response to pH variations, confirming their applicability as visual indicators for food freshness and quality monitoring. The incorporation of anthocyanin extract significantly influenced the films’ physical, barrier, and mechanical properties, improving their strength and flexibility ( p  < 0.05). The FE showed a higher total phenolic content (1400.65 mg GAE/100 g), anthocyanin content (375.28 mg/100 g), and significantly greater antioxidant capacity compared to the control film (FC). The overall migration of film constituents was considerably higher in water than in acetic acid and ethanol. Morphological and structural analyses revealed that anthocyanin extract did not substantially alter the film’s surface or cause significant structural changes in the pectin matrix. Still, it exhibited the highest melting temperature (253.64 °C). Changes in total volatile basic nitrogen (TVB-N) content and pH fluctuations affected the film’s color response. Finally, the findings of this study demonstrated that the fabricated pH indicator film is pH-sensitive and can be used to monitor shrimp freshness. Graphical Abstract
journal: Journal of Food Measurement and Characterization

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Due to the high global production and processing of citrus fruits, large volumes of by-products and waste are generated, causing significant disposal management issues and representing a high economic cost for the citrus industry Krivošija et al. [ 1 ]. The principles of green chemistry offer an efficient approach to utilizing citrus fruit waste, transforming it into value-added materials Guliani et al. [ 2 ]. Oranges are among the most consumed fruits worldwide, with an annual production exceeding 75 million tons in 2021. During their processing, various by-products, such as peels, pulp, and seeds, are generated and require proper management Li et al. [ 3 ]. Current orange waste management practices are limited to low-value applications, such as animal feed, composting, and landfill disposal, leading to a high environmental impact. In response, research has focused on the valorization of these residues, aiming to recover free sugars, essential oils, pectin, and bioactive compounds such as flavonoids and polyphenols Giannakis et al. [ 4 ].

Although orange peel ( Citrus sinensis ) is often treated as a byproduct in the agro-industrial industry, it is a rich source of flavonoids. These bioactive phenolic compounds possess several properties, such as antioxidant Gupta et al. [ 5 ], antimicrobial Lai et al. [ 6 ], anti-inflammatory Guo et al. [ 7 ], anticancer Hamai et al. [ 8 ], and anti-atherosclerotic Liu et al., [ 9 ] Peron et al. [ 10 ]. These properties make them suitable for various industrial applications, including inhibiting lipid oxidation in meats and extending shelf life in perishable products when incorporated into food packaging and films Niglio et al. [ 11 ].

The high pectin content in orange peels, ranging from 30% to 45%, provides an excellent film-forming capacity, enabling the production of films predominantly made from this agro-industrial byproduct Quilez-Molina et al. [ 12 ]. The valorization of orange peels for pectin extraction has become increasingly relevant, as this process contributes to reducing the volume of waste generated while offering an alternative to synthetic compounds Iñiguez-Moreno et al. [ 13 ]. Pectin-based packaging materials stand out for their oxygen barrier properties, intrinsic bioactivity, compatibility with other biopolymers, and cost-effectiveness. In addition to being readily biodegradable, these materials extend the shelf life of food, improve its quality, and act as practical barriers, thus allowing for the controlled release of ingredients and regulating gas and moisture exchange Bocker e Silva, [ 14 ].

Intelligent films, characterized by their small size, low cost, and rapid accuracy, present a promising strategy for providing real-time information on the quality of meat and fish products. These films typically contain a solid matrix containing a pH-sensitive dye. This dye reacts with the metabolites of the food product, causing a color change that facilitates the monitoring of freshness. Compared to synthetic dyes, anthocyanins (natural indicators) are more suitable due to their safety, environmental sustainability, and high sensitivity to pH Huang et al. [ 15 ]. In this context, purple-fleshed sweet potato stands out as an excellent source of anthocyanins, as it contains high concentrations of these pigments responsible for its intense purple coloration. This tuber is also widely available and has a bioactive profile associated with antioxidant properties, making it a natural and functional alternative for incorporating into intelligent films Da Silva et al. [ 16 ].

This study aimed to develop biodegradable films using pectin from orange peel residues, purple-fleshed sweet potato extract, and glycerol, with potential application for food freshness monitoring. The study evaluated the physical, barrier, mechanical, bioactive, antioxidant, morphological, structural, and thermal properties of the developed material and its feasibility as a freshness indicator for shrimp. Using agro-industrial residues in packaging formulation presents a promising solution to drive the sector forward. By repurposing these abundant byproducts, it is possible to reduce waste, utilize renewable resources, and significantly contribute to reducing environmental pollution, fostering a more sustainable packaging system.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Orange peels ( Citrus sinensis ) provided by a fruit processing industry located in Campina Grande, Paraíba, Brazil, were used as the raw material for pectin extraction. Purple-fleshed sweet potatoes ( Ipomoea batatas  [L.] Lam.) were purchased from the Paraíba Supply and Agricultural Services Company (EMPASA) in Campina Grande, Paraíba, Brazil. Ethanol (96%, v/v), glycerol, and hydrochloric acid were obtained from Neon Química (São Paulo, Brazil).

The reagents TPTZ (2,4,6-Tri(2-pyridyl)-s-triazine), Trolox (6-hydroxy-2,5,7,8-tetramethylchroman-2-carboxylic acid), 2,2’-azinobis (3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS), 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH), ferric chloride hexahydrate, hydrochloric acid, and Folin-Ciocalteu were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Additionally, 96% ethanol and analytical-grade sodium chloride were acquired from NEON (Suzano, São Paulo, Brazil). Ultrapure water was obtained using a purification system from Marte Científica (São Paulo, Brazil). Potassium persulfate, phosphoric acid, ferrous sulfate, and monobasic potassium phosphate were purchased from Merck (Darmstadt, Germany).

sections.heading: Pectin extraction
paragraphs: Pectin extraction was performed through acid hydrolysis following the method described by Siddiqui, Chand, and Shahi [ 17 ],, with some modifications. For this process, 1 kg of orange peels (previously washed with water and sanitized using a hypochlorous acid (HClO) solution at 200 mg/L for 5 min) was suspended in distilled water acidified to pH 2.0 with 1.5 mol L⁻¹ HCl, using a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:10 (w/v). The mixture was autoclaved at 150 °C and 120 kPa for 15 min.

After cooling to 25 °C, the acidic extract was filtered using a synthetic nylon fabric, allowing the gradual separation of suspended solids. The aqueous extract containing pectin was precipitated with 96% ethanol (1:1, w/v) and kept at 4 °C for 24 h. The gelatinous pectin was then filtered again, washed with 96% ethanol, and subsequently with distilled water. Finally, the gelatinous pectin underwent convective drying in a laboratory oven at 40 °C for 24 h. The resulting powdered pectin was stored in zip-lock bags at 4 °C until further use.

sections.heading: Extraction yield
Equivalent weight
paragraphs: The equivalent weight of pectin was determined by titration following the method described by Ranganna [ 18 ]. First, 0.5 g of pectin was weighed, and 5 mL of ethanol was added to the sample. Then, 1 g of analytical-grade sodium chloride was incorporated to assist in the endpoint detection of the titration. Additionally, 100 mL of distilled water was added to the mixture. After homogenization, six drops of phenol red were used as an indicator.

sections.heading: Methoxyl content
paragraphs: The determination of methoxyl content was performed through the saponification of pectin followed by the titration of the liberated carboxyl groups, as described by Ranganna [ 18 ]. The neutralized solution obtained during the equivalent weight determination was collected, and 25 mL of 0.25 mol·L⁻¹ NaOH was added. The mixture was then thoroughly stirred and kept at room temperature for 30 min.

sections.heading: Extraction of anthocyanins from purple-fleshed sweet potato
paragraphs: The extraction of anthocyanins from purple-fleshed sweet potatoes was carried out following the procedures described by Guo et al. [ 19 ] and Dong et al. [ 20 ], with minor modifications. The sweet potatoes were sanitized using a sodium hypochlorite solution (200 mg of active chlorine/L) for 15 min and then rinsed with running water.

Next, 10 g of sweet potato was weighed and mixed with 100 mL of distilled water (H₂O), adjusted to pH 3.0 with 1.5 mol·L⁻¹ HCl, and heated to 95 °C for 5 min. After this period, the resulting solution was filtered using blue-band filter paper to obtain a clear anthocyanin solution. The filtered anthocyanin solution was stored in a freezer at 4 °C until use, while the residue retained on the filter paper was discarded.

sections.heading: Film preparation
paragraphs: The methodology for film production was based on the solution casting process described by Roy et al. [ 21 ]. In the formulation of the control film (FC), 10 g of pectin was dissolved in 40 mL of distilled water, to which 2 g of glycerol was added as a plasticizer. The solution was heated to 90 °C on a hot plate and vigorously stirred for approximately 1 h to ensure complete dissolution of the pectin.

For the formulation containing extract (FE), 10 g of pectin was dissolved in 2 g of glycerol under the same stirring and temperature conditions. After complete homogenization, 40 mL of anthocyanin extract (as determined in preliminary tests) was added.

The solutions were poured onto glass plates coated with petroleum jelly to facilitate film removal. The films were dried at room temperature for 24 h in a desiccator until characterization tests were performed. All experiments were conducted in triplicate to ensure consistency and reproducibility of results.

sections.heading: Response of films to pH variation
paragraphs: The pH responsiveness of the FE films was tested according to the method described by Alizadeh-Sani et al. [ 22 ], with some modifications. At 25 ± 1 °C, the indicator films were cut into 3 cm × 3 cm pieces and immersed in buffer solutions with pH values of 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 12 for 1 min. After immersion, the films were removed, and excess buffer solution was absorbed by filter paper.

Color analysis of the films was performed using a portable colorimeter (FRU ® , WR10QC, Hangzhou, China) with a precision of 0.01 units and a repeatability of 0.08. The color values were expressed in the CIELAB scale, where L* represents lightness, a* indicates the intensity from green (-) to red (+), and b* indicates the intensity from blue (-) to yellow (+).

sections.heading: Water content, water activity (aw) and thickness
paragraphs: The water content of the films was determined as described by Latimer [ 23 ] through drying at 105 °C until constant weight was achieved. A water activity meter (Aqualab, Decagon, Pullman, WA, USA) was used to measure the water activity (aw) of the films.

The thickness of the samples was measured using a digital micrometer (Stanley ® , Digital Caliper 78440LA, New Britain, Connecticut, USA). Measurements were taken at three random points on each sample to calculate an average thickness.

sections.heading: Solubility
paragraphs: The films’ Solubility was determined using a gravimetric method. For this, 1 g of each sample was added to 100 mL of distilled water and stirred on a magnetic stirrer for 5 min at room temperature. Afterward, the samples were centrifuged at 3,000 rpm for 5 min, and the supernatant was transferred to an evaporation dish that had been previously weighed. The dish was then dried at 105 °C until constant weight was achieved.

sections.heading: Water vapor transmission rate (WVTR)
paragraphs: Where WVTR is the water vapor transmission rate, g/(m·s·Pa); Δ_m is the amount of moisture passing through the composite film (g); χ is the thickness of the composite film (mm); t is the time for water to penetrate the composite film (h); A is the transmission area of the composite film (m²); ΔP is the difference in water vapor pressure on both sides of the composite film (Pa).

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: The mechanical properties were analyzed according to method ASTM D828-97 [ 25 ], using a TA TX Plus texture analyzer (Stable Micro Systems, Surrey, UK). The samples (dimensions of 20 × 40 mm) were cut from the center of the composites and subjected to tensile tests at a rate of 0.42 mm/s. The initial separation of the grips was 30 mm, and the test was performed until film rupture. The rupture strength, elongation at rupture, and the elastic modulus were obtained directly from the tangent in the linear region of the curve.

sections.heading: Total phenolic compounds
paragraphs: The total phenolic content of the films was quantified using the Folin-Ciocalteu method, as described by Waterhouse [ 26 ]. For the preparation of the extracts, 1 g of the films was mixed with 50 mL of an ethanol-water solution (80:20, v/v) and subjected to ultrasonic bath in an ultrasonic cleaner (Cristofoli ® , Campos Mourão, Paraná, Brazil) at 42 kHz for 30 min, protected from light. The solutions were then filtered using filter paper.

The quantification of total phenolic compounds was performed based on a standard curve of gallic acid with concentrations ranging from 0 to 225 µg/mL, and readings were made using a spectrophotometer at 765 nm. The results were expressed as milligrams of gallic acid equivalent (GAE) per kilogram of film (mg GAE/100 g).

sections.heading: Anthocyanins
paragraphs: The determination of total anthocyanin content in the films was carried out following the method described by Francis [ 27 ]. For the extract preparation, 1 g of each film formulation was ground in a solution of ethanol–HCl at 1.5 mol/L in a 85:15 (v/v) ratio. The samples were then stored in a refrigerator (Consul ® , São Paulo, Brazil) at −10 °C for 24 h. After this period, the extract was filtered, and readings were made using a spectrophotometer at a wavelength of 535 nm, specific for the quantification of anthocyanins. The results were expressed as milligrams of total anthocyanins per kilogram of film (mg/100 g).

sections.heading: Antioxidant activity (DPPH, FRAP, ABTS)
paragraphs: For the determination of antioxidant capacity, three methods were employed: DPPH radical scavenging, ABTS Re, Kim [ 28 ,  29 ], and the Ferric Reducing Antioxidant Power (FRAP) assay Rufino [ 30 ]. First, extracts of each sample were prepared as described earlier in the methodology for determining phenolic compounds (item 2.5.3).

The ABTS radical was generated by reacting a 7 mM ABTS solution with 140 mM potassium persulfate, incubated in a water bath at 27 °C, in the dark, for 16 h. The radical was then diluted in ethanol to achieve an absorbance of 0.700 ± 0.050 at 734 nm. In the dark, 300 µL of the extract were mixed with 2700 µL of the radical, and readings were taken after 6 min of reaction at 734 nm. The analytical curve was constructed using Trolox. The results were expressed as percentage inhibition.

The FRAP reagent was prepared by mixing 25 mL of acetate buffer solution (300 mM, pH 3.6), 2.5 mL of TPTZ solution (10 mM in 40 mM HCl), and 2.5 mL of FeCl₃ solution (20 mM). For analysis, 90 µL of the sample extract were mixed with 270 µL of deionized water and 2.7 mL of FRAP solution, and the mixture was incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. The absorbance was measured at 595 nm using a spectrophotometer, with a blank reagent used to zero the absorbance. The analytical curve was constructed using ferrous sulfate, and the results were expressed as µM Fe²⁺/g of film.

sections.heading: Migration performance
paragraphs: The films were immersed in 5 mL of a 3% acetic acid solution (to simulate an acidic food), water (to simulate a neutral food), a 10% ethanol solution (to simulate an alcoholic food), and 95% ethanol (to simulate a fatty food). The supernatants were then analyzed for TPC (Sect.  2.5.4 ) and anthocyanins (Sect.  2.5.5 ) to evaluate the migration into simulated food fluids.

sections.heading: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
paragraphs: The surface microstructure of the films was analyzed using a scanning electron microscope (VEGA3 TESCAN, Massachusetts, USA) operating at 10 kV and a magnification of 1000×. All samples were properly dried, mounted on aluminum stubs with carbon adhesive tape, and gold-coated in an argon atmosphere.

sections.heading: Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) absorption spectroscopy
paragraphs: The FT-IR spectra were obtained using a spectrometer (model Vertex 70, BRUKER) in the range of 4000 to 400 cm⁻¹, with 64 scans. The FT-IR spectra were recorded in absorbance over the wavenumber range.

sections.heading: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC)
paragraphs: The thermal properties of the films were analyzed using a differential scanning calorimeter (DSC Q20, TA Instruments – Waters LLC, New Castle, USA). For this, a 5 mg sample was carefully weighed and placed in an alumina crucible (TA Instruments – Waters LLC, New Castle, USA), which was hermetically sealed. The crucible was equilibrated in a refrigerated environment at 4 °C for 12 h before being subjected to a controlled heating process, ranging from 50 to 350 °C at a rate of 10 °C/min.

sections.heading: Monitoring the freshness of shrimp
paragraphs: The film containing the anthocyanin extract (FE) was used to monitor the freshness of shrimp. For this, approximately 10 g portions of fresh shrimp were placed in sterile containers covered with lids and stored at 25 °C and 4 °C for 48 h. The pre-cut FE film, with dimensions of 2 × 4 cm, was directly placed inside the packaging, and changes in the color of the film were observed at 0, 12, 24, and 48 h. The freshness of the shrimp was evaluated using total nitrogen by the micro-Kjeldahl method to determine the nitrogen content of the samples, with the nitrogen-to-protein conversion factor of 6.25, as determined by Latimer Jr [ 23 ],. pH measurements were taken by suspending 5 g of shrimp in 10 mL of distilled water and agitating for 30 min. After that, the pH was directly measured using a pH meter (Bench pH Meter - mPA-210 - MS Tecnopon), and microbiological analysis was performed by counting the population of  Pseudomonas spp . in shrimp samples during storage, determined according to the methodology described by Dabade et al. [ 31 ], with slight modifications. Briefly, 10 g of shrimp sample were aseptically transferred to a sterile homogenizer bag containing 90 mL of sterile peptone water (0.1% w/v) and homogenized for 2 min. Serial decimal dilutions were prepared using sterile peptone water. Aliquots (0.1 mL) of the appropriate dilutions were plated on Pseudomonas base agar supplemented with a selective CFC supplement (cetrimide, fucidin, and cephaloridine). The inoculated plates were incubated aerobically at 25 °C for 48 h. After incubation, characteristic colonies of Pseudomonas spp. Counts were obtained and the results expressed as log CFU/g of shrimp sample. All analyses were performed in triplicate and the results were presented as mean ± standard deviation.

sections.heading: Statistical analysis
paragraphs: The results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. All analyses were performed in triplicate ( n  = 3), and differences between the means were determined by analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Tukey’s test, with a 95% confidence interval ( p  ≤ 0.05). The  Statistic  7.0 software (Tibco, Statistica, Palo Alto, CA, USA) was used for these analyses.

sections.heading: Characterization of extracted pectin
paragraphs: The results for yield, equivalent weight, and methoxyl content of pectin extracted from orange peels show high and consistent values, indicating the quality of the obtained biopolymer. The extraction yield reached 45.44% ± 3.23, a considerably high value, suggesting the efficiency of the process and the adequacy of the experimental conditions, particularly the use of a low pH solvent. The acidity promotes the solubilization and recovery of pectin, minimizing losses and maximizing extraction from the orange peel residue. This high yield highlights the potential of the residue as a viable and sustainable source of pectin for industrial applications. High extraction yields were also reported by Demir et al. [ 32 ] for pectin from lemon peel and by Kamal et al. (2021) [ 33 ] for pectin from sweet orange peel ( Citrus sinensis ).

The equivalent weight of the extracted pectin was 1807.76 g ± 3.8, a value very close to the range reported by Kamal et al. [ 33 ] (1744.66–1899.33 g) for citrus pectin extracted from  Citrus sinensis . This parameter reflects the molecular weight of pectin and its structural integrity, serving as an indicator of the preservation of the polymer chain during the extraction process. The similarity in values suggests that the method used minimized the degradation of the biopolymer, allowing for the production of pectin with an appropriate structure for various technological applications, such as thickening, gelling, and stabilizing agents in food and pharmaceutical formulations Wang [ 34 ].

The methoxyl content of the extracted pectin was 79.26% ± 1.53, demonstrating a high degree of esterification. This value is higher than the range found by Kamal et al. [ 33 ] (73.26% − 77.56%) for citrus pectin, suggesting that the extraction conditions favored the preservation of the methoxyl groups. High methoxylation is a key factor for gelation properties, water retention, and interaction with other components, making it essential for industrial applications in food systems, such as jams and dairy products, as well as potential use in biodegradable films and coatings Siddiqui [ 17 ]. Overall, our results indicate that the pectin extracted from orange peel has characteristics comparable to pectin extracted from other sources, reinforcing the potential of this waste as a sustainable raw material for developing new products and industrial applications.

sections.heading: Evaluation of color based on pH variation
paragraphs: The pH of a food is directly related to its quality, freshness, and safety, and it may change during storage. Therefore, pH measurement can be used as an effective method for monitoring changes in these essential aspects of packaged foods Khan [ 35 ]. Smart films containing anthocyanins have the ability to change color predictably in response to pH variations, due to the structural transitions of these molecules, as evidenced by Fang et al. [ 36 ] in Fig.  1 . In this study, the functionality of films containing purple-fleshed sweet potato extract (FE) was evaluated as pH sensors, using different buffer solutions. The color parameters (L*, a*, and b*) of the films are presented in Table  1 . Fig. 1 Changes in the chemical structure of anthocyanins at different pH’s Fonte: Fang et al. [ 36 ] Table 1 Actual color changes of the pectin-based film from orange peel, glycerol, and purple-fleshed sweet potato anthocyanin extract according to buffer solutions

The color change of the films at pH 4.0 to 6.0 showed subtle visual differences, indicating that in this range, the anthocyanins maintain relatively stable structures. In an acidic medium (pH 2–6), the films exhibited a reddish color, characteristic of the cationic flavilium form of anthocyanins. As the pH increased, the color of the film underwent progressive changes, becoming bluish around pH 8 (pseudo-base of carbinol) and eventually yellow-green in an alkaline pH (pH 10–12) due to the conversion to the chalcone form Roy [ 21 ].

The L* value was relatively high for films submerged in buffer solutions with pH values ranging from 2 to 10, suggesting that the clarity of the color was preserved within this range ( p  < 0.05). The* value (indicating redness) rapidly decreased as the pH increased, indicating the loss of the intense red color characteristic of the acidic medium. This behavior was accompanied by a decrease in the b* value (indicating yellowness) ( p  < 0.05), reinforcing the gradual transition of the anthocyanins to structural states associated with higher pH values. This behavior was also previously reported by Ji et al. [ 37 ] for films based on pectin/sodium carboxymethyl cellulose/anthocyanin with added Zhongke Blue 1 extract from blue honeysuckle berries. These results demonstrate that the films developed in this study have a predictable and responsive color change to pH variations, confirming their potential applicability as visual indicators for monitoring food freshness and quality.

sections.heading: Physical, barrier, and mechanical properties of the films
paragraphs: The incorporation of purple-fleshed sweet potato anthocyanin extract significantly influenced the physical, barrier, and mechanical properties of films based on orange peel pectin and glycerol, as shown in Table  2 . The water content of the films showed a slight reduction with the addition of the extract compared to the control film (FC) ( p  < 0.05). This decrease may be associated with the interaction between the anthocyanins and the polymeric pectin matrix, reducing the availability of free hydrophilic groups for water retention. However, the water activity (aw) did not show statistically significant differences between the control film (FC) and the anthocyanin extract film (FE) ( p  > 0.05), suggesting that despite the lower moisture content, both films exhibit similar behavior in terms of water availability in the system. This behavior has also been reported for starch-based films with the addition of pitaya peel Santos [ 38 ]. Letters (a, b) different in the same row indicate statistically significant differences between formulations according to the Tukey test

It is important to note that the purple sweet potato extract used in this study is a complex natural matrix composed not only of anthocyanins but also of sugars, organic acids, minerals, and other soluble constituents. Therefore, the differences observed between the control film (FC) and the extract-containing film (FE) cannot be attributed exclusively to anthocyanins. These additional components may also interact with the pectin matrix, influencing the physical, barrier, mechanical, and antioxidant properties of the films. Nevertheless, the use of the whole extract was intentionally adopted as a sustainable and cost-effective approach for the development of intelligent packaging materials, allowing the synergistic action of naturally occurring compounds present in purple sweet potato.

The increase in thickness in the anthocyanin extract film (FE) compared to the control film (FC) ( p  < 0.05) can be attributed to the incorporation of bioactive compounds and the potential interactions between the anthocyanins and the pectin polymer network, promoting a structural rearrangement. This factor may have contributed to the increase in the solubility of the films, as the FE showed a higher value (68.33%) compared to the FC (65.26%) ( p  < 0.05). This effect may be related to anthocyanins, which have a hydrophilic nature, favoring the solubilization of the film in an aqueous medium Khan [ 39 ]. The Water Vapor Transmission Rate (WVTR) was slightly lower for FE (0.24 × 10 − 10  g/(m·s·Pa)) compared to FC (0.28 × 10 − 10  g/(m·s·Pa)). Although this difference was not statistically significant ( p  > 0.05), the slight reduction suggests a positive effect of incorporating anthocyanins into the film structure, possibly strengthening its polymer matrix and hindering water vapor transmission. This indicates that interactions between pectin and the compounds from the extract may have increased the structural cohesion of the film, reducing its permeability. In contrast, Dong et al. [ 20 ] observed that the WVTR of a chitosan-based film loaded with quercetin containing purple sweet potato anthocyanins was higher (1.5 × 10 − 9  g/(m·s·Pa)) than the FE film in this study.

The results of the mechanical properties (Table  2 ) indicate that the incorporation of the anthocyanin extract into the film (FE) led to significant improvements in the film’s strength and flexibility compared to the control (FC) ( p  < 0.05). The tensile strength increased dramatically, from 2.52 MPa (FC) to 4.35 MPa (FE), suggesting that the addition of the extract contributed to the formation of a more cohesive and resistant matrix, as observed by Santos et al. [ 38 ]. The increase in the elastic modulus, from 19.64 MPa to 29.83 MPa, further supports this hypothesis, indicating that the FE exhibited a more rigid structure, possibly due to the formation of additional interactions between the phenolic compounds of the extract and the polymer matrix. This structural reinforcement may be related to the strengthening of hydrogen bonds between the polyphenols and the pectin chains, as reported in previous studies Wang [ 40 ].

Furthermore, the elongation at break nearly doubled in the FE (0.23%) compared to the FC (0.10%), demonstrating that films containing anthocyanins have greater deformation capacity before rupture. This effect may be related to the high content of polyphenols and sugars present in the extract, which can act as natural plasticizers, increasing the mobility of the polymer chains and improving the material’s flexibility Li et al. [ 3 ]. This behavior is consistent with studies showing that incorporating plant extracts can strengthen polymer films through hydrogen bonds and dipole-ion interactions between the hydroxyl groups of polyphenols and the galacturonic acid residues of pectin [ 41 ]. Additionally, Zeng et al. [ 42 ] reported that the increase in phenolic, flavonoid, and anthocyanin content could promote crosslinking between polymer chains, resulting in films that are both more resistant and flexible.

It is essential to highlight that variations in the mechanical properties of biopolymeric films incorporated with plant extracts are common, as the chemical composition of the extracts can interfere with the physical interactions within the polymeric matrix Mir [ 43 ]. In this study, the high values of elongation at break in the FE suggest that anthocyanins also played a plasticizing role, reducing excessive rigidity and allowing for more significant deformation before rupture. Therefore, our findings indicate that adding purple sweet potato pulp anthocyanin extract not only improved the mechanical strength of the film but also optimized its balance between rigidity and flexibility, which can be advantageous for applications in biodegradable and innovative packaging.

sections.heading: Total phenolic compounds, anthocyanins, and antioxidant capacity
paragraphs: The total phenolic compounds (TPC), anthocyanins, and antioxidant potential of the developed films were evaluated and are presented in Fig.  2 . The purple sweet potato pulp anthocyanin extract showed a TPC of 925.47 mg GAE/100 g and anthocyanins of 375.88 mg/100 g. Its incorporation into the polymeric matrix significantly influenced the bioactive and antioxidant properties of the film ( p  < 0.05). The incorporation of the anthocyanin extract significantly increased the total phenolic content and anthocyanin concentration of the films compared to the control formulation ( p  < 0.05), reflecting the successful enrichment of the pectin matrix with bioactive compounds (Figs.  2 A and  2 B). This increase can be attributed to the presence of phenolic hydroxyl groups, which play a key role in the structural stability of bioactive compounds and in the ability to donate and accept protons. According to the Brønsted-Lowry acid-base theory, phenolic hydroxyl groups exhibit amphoteric behavior, meaning they can act as both proton donors and acceptors depending on the pH of the medium Zeng [ 42 ]. Fig. 2 Total phenolic content ( A ), anthocyanins ( B ), and antioxidant potential: DPPH ( C ), ABTS ( D ), and FRAP ( E ) of films based on orange peel pectin, glycerol, and purple sweet potato anthocyanin extract. Bars with different letters ( a ,  b ) indicate statistically significant differences between the films according to the Tukey test

This effect is also related to the color variation observed in the FE films. The color of films containing anthocyanins can change due to alterations in the electronic distribution along the phenolic rings, resulting in the modulation of the chromophore group Zeng [ 42 ]. These interactions promote the formation of conjugated double bonds, which generate different hues, as presented in Table  1 .

Bioactive films incorporated with plant extracts may exhibit antioxidant activity, neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS) and free radicals generated during food storage and consumption. This effect is particularly relevant for extending the oxidative stability of packaged products, reducing deterioration processes, and increasing their shelf life Khan [ 35 ].

To evaluate the antioxidant potential of the developed films, DPPH radical scavenging assays (Fig.  2 C), ABTS (Fig.  2 D), and FRAP (Fig.  2 E) were performed. As expected, the results show that the FC exhibited low antioxidant activity in all methods analyzed since its formulation does not contain the anthocyanin extract. In contrast, the FE demonstrated a significantly superior capacity for free radical scavenging, reaching 97.60% in the DPPH assay and 94.74% in the ABTS assay, in addition to a reducing potential of 801.20 µM Fe²⁺/g in the FRAP assay ( p  < 0.05).

These results are consistent with previous studies, such as the one by Guo et al. [ 19 ], which reported a DPPH scavenging activity of 75.29% upon incorporating 2.0% purple cabbage extract into polymer films. This suggests that the extract in the present study has even more significant antioxidant potential, possibly due to the higher concentration of anthocyanins and other bioactive compounds in purple sweet potato. The high antioxidant activity of the FE is attributed to the presence of anthocyanins from purple sweet potato, phenolic compounds widely recognized for their electron-donating ability, free radical neutralization, and stabilization of oxidative species.

In addition to protecting packaged foods against oxidation, the FE’s high antioxidant capacity may bring additional benefits, such as preserving sensory and nutritional compounds in products, preventing lipid degradation, and preventing the formation of undesirable compounds. Therefore, incorporating plant extracts rich in anthocyanins could be a promising strategy for developing active and intelligent packaging, enhancing the functionality of films, and making them a sustainable alternative for food preservation.

sections.heading: Migration in simulated media
paragraphs: An ideal food packaging material should be inert, meaning it should not release its constituents into food in quantities that compromise its safety or quality Narasagoudr [ 44 ]. The migration of constituents from the polymeric matrix of the films was evaluated in different simulated media, and the results are shown in Fig.  3 . It was observed that the overall migration was significantly higher in water compared to acetic acid and ethanol. This can be explained by the highly water-soluble nature of pectin, which is the main component of both the FC and FE films. Pectin has a greater affinity for water due to its hydrophilic properties, facilitating its dissolution in this medium. This resulted in a significantly higher overall migration in water, with FE showing 430.45 ± 4.8 µg/kg of migration, while FC had 400.76 ± 5.6 µg/kg ( p  < 0.05). The higher migration in FE can be attributed to the superior solubility of the bioactive compounds in this film in water, which facilitates their release from the matrix. Fig. 3 Overall migration index of the developed films in different simulant media (water, alcohol, and acetic acid). FC: control film without the addition of anthocyanin extract; FE: film with the addition of purple sweet potato anthocyanin extract. Bars with different letters ( a ,  b ,  c ) indicate statistically significant differences between the media for the same film according to the Tukey test; Bars with different letters ( A ,  B ) indicate statistically significant differences between the films for the same medium according to the Tukey test

On the other hand, the migration in ethanol was considerably lower for both films, with FC showing 55.6 ± 2.5 µg/kg and FE 40.66 ± 5.6 µg/kg. This can be attributed to the more compact microstructure of the films, which hinders the release of constituents into ethanol. Additionally, the low solubility of pectin in ethanol contributes to lower migration of compounds in this medium, as pectin interacts less favorably with ethanol. Finally, 3% acetic acid migration was lower than in water but still higher than in ethanol. FE showed 180.54 ± 3.6 µg/kg, while FC showed 150.78 ± 2.8 µg/kg, with a significant difference between the films. The higher migration in FE in acetic acid can be explained by the higher solubility of bioactive compounds in an acidic medium, which facilitates the release of the phenolic compounds and anthocyanins in the film Santos et al. [ 38 ]. When developing pectin-based films, Goudar et al. [ 45 ] found a higher migration rate in water, followed by ethanol and acetic acid.

These results indicate that the nature of the simulated medium significantly impacts the migration of constituents from the films and that the presence of bioactive compounds in FE may influence this migration, particularly in aqueous or acidic environments.

sections.heading: Morphological, structural and thermal properties
paragraphs: Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) images of the surfaces of FC and FE films (Fig.  4 A) were analyzed to investigate their microstructures, revealing a porous, rough, and irregular structure, characteristic of the mixture of components used in the formulation. However, the addition of the anthocyanin extract did not result in significant visual differences in the surface of the films, indicating that the incorporation of bioactive compounds did not substantially alter the topography of the polymer matrix. These results are consistent with those found by Rohela et al. [ 46 ] and Shivangi et al. [ 47 ], who also investigated pectin-based films containing plant extracts. Both studies observed that the addition of plant extracts, including bioactive compounds, did not significantly alter the surface morphology of the films but did result in visible porosity and roughness. This behavior may be attributed to the interaction of the extracts with the pectin matrix, which may create similar microstructures without causing visible changes. Fig. 4 SEM micrographs ( A ), FT-IR spectra ( B ), and DSC thermograms ( C ) of films based on orange peel pectin, glycerol, and purple sweet potato anthocyanin extract

The FT-IR spectra (Fig.  4 B) were used to investigate the intermolecular interactions and potential structural changes in the pectin films after the introduction of the anthocyanin extract. Overall, the analysis revealed that adding the anthocyanin extract did not induce the formation of new functional groups in the films, as both the FC and FE exhibited similar peaks (3420, 2980, 1612, and 1050 cm − 1 ) and a broad absorption region. According to Cabello et al. (2015) [ 48 ], peaks around 3400 cm − 1  are attributed to the stretching vibration of -OH bonds within the pectin monomers Wathoni [ 49 ]. The peak around 2927 cm − 1  corresponds to the stretching vibration of -CH bonds from methylene groups in pectin chains and methyl ester groups [ 21 ]. The peak around 1010 cm − 1  refers to the COC stretching vibrations in the polymer chain structure, as pectin samples typically show a weaker symmetric COO− stretching followed by moderately intense absorption patterns between 1300 and 800 cm − 1 , collectively referred to as the “fingerprint” region, which is unique to a compound Ellerbrock [ 50 ].

These results indicate that the introduction of the anthocyanin extract did not promote significant structural changes in the pectin, as no new peaks or shifts in characteristic peaks were observed, suggesting that there were no strong chemical interactions between the bioactive compounds and the pectin matrix sufficient to alter the polymer’s molecular structure. However, it is possible that weaker intermolecular interactions, such as hydrogen bonds between the hydroxyl groups of the anthocyanins and the functional groups of pectin, may have occurred. This could explain the improvements in the functional properties of the film, such as mechanical strength and antioxidant activity, without causing obvious structural changes.

The endothermic behavior of all thermograms was analyzed in the temperature range of 50–350 °C (Fig.  4 C). The primary degradation of the FE and FC films occurred at temperatures of 150.75 °C and 160.12 °C, respectively, indicating the initial thermal stability of the film before the onset of more pronounced degradation. Regarding the melting temperature, the peak was observed at 253.64 °C for the FE film and at 240.77 °C for the FC film. The melting temperature of FE was significantly higher than that of FC, which can be attributed to incorporating the anthocyanin extract, which promoted more excellent thermal stability. This increase in the melting temperature can be explained by the efficient integration of the anthocyanin extract into the pectin polymer network, resulting in a more cohesive and structured matrix with higher resistance to melting. The interactions between the phenolic compounds of the extract and the functional groups of pectin may have provided greater crosslinking of the film structure, hindered melting and increased thermal stability [ 51 ].

Previous studies, such as the one by Mehraj et al. [ 52 ], reported melting temperatures ranging from 106 °C to 165 °C for pectin films incorporated with  Terminalia catappa Linn . leaf wax and xylitol, showing a broader range compared to our results. The presence of a single melting peak in our films suggests that the composite films (FE and FC) are miscible with each other, indicating that the anthocyanin extract was homogeneously incorporated into the pectin matrix, forming a single phase without component segregation.

sections.heading: Application of the film in monitoring shrimp freshness
paragraphs: A color analysis was conducted during the shrimp deterioration process to explore the potential of the anthocyanin-enriched film (FE) as a freshness indicator. The FE, due to the presence of anthocyanins, can react with the volatile compounds and biochemical processes released during seafood spoilage. Tables  3  and  4  presents the results of the color analysis of the films during shrimp freshness monitoring under conditions of 25 and 4 °C. The FE films, enriched with anthocyanin extract, significantly varied color parameters during the shrimp deterioration process ( p  < 0.05). Table 3 Effect of packaging films on shrimp quality during storage for 48 hours at 25 °C Table 4 Effect of packaging films on shrimp quality during storage for 48 hours at 4 °C

At the early time points (0 and 12 h), the values of a* were elevated, associated with the red color characteristic of anthocyanins. These changes in the film’s color parameters indicated that contact with compounds released during seafood deterioration altered the film’s color, reflecting the product’s degradation. In particular, the values of a* decreased, showing a color change from red to green, which can be attributed to the chemical conversion of anthocyanins in response to the volatile compounds released.

The analysis of the b* values showed a more complex behavior, decreasing from 9.7 to 7.5 between 0 and 48 h and a maximum peak of 12.8 at 12 h. This behavior can be explained by the interaction of the anthocyanins with volatile compounds, such as ammonia (NH 3 ), which alters the chemical structure of the extract. As described by Zhai et al. [ 53 ], the mechanism of color variation in intelligent films may be related to the interaction of volatile NH 3  with the water incorporated into the film, producing NH 4+  and OH −  ions. These hydroxide ions create an alkaline environment that favors the conversion of anthocyanins into chalcones, which in turn causes a color change in the film, as illustrated in Fig.  1 .

Additionally, an increase in the L* value was observed over time, indicating a tendency for the film to become lighter as the seafood deteriorated. This behavior suggests that the film exhibited good color perception, making the changes visible to the naked eye. According to Mohammadalinejhad [ 54 ], shrimp is particularly susceptible to deterioration due to its high protein, fat, and moisture content. During storage, proteolytic enzymes break down proteins, and microorganisms present in the environment further decompose proteins and amino acids, releasing volatile nitrogen compounds such as ammonia (NH 3 ), dimethylamine (DMA), and trimethylamine (TMA). These volatile gases accumulate inside the packaging, leading to a gradual increase in pH, which can be monitored by colorimetric sensors sensitive to pH changes.

To further evaluate the applicability of the intelligent film under realistic storage conditions, shrimp freshness was also monitored at 4 °C for 48 h (Table  4 ). The FE film exhibited progressive and statistically significant changes in its color parameters during refrigerated storage ( p  < 0.05). The L* value increased from 25.25 to 28.22, indicating a slight increase in film lightness over time. More pronounced changes were observed for the a* and b* parameters, which increased from 23.62 to 41.58 and from 13.91 to 28.44, respectively. These variations indicate that the film remained sensitive to the biochemical changes occurring in the shrimp even under refrigerated conditions, although spoilage reactions were slower than those observed at 25 °C. The visible color modifications observed throughout storage demonstrate that the anthocyanin-containing film can effectively respond to changes associated with seafood deterioration under refrigeration, supporting its potential application as a real-time freshness indicator in practical cold-chain storage conditions.

Figure  5  illustrates the evolution of the volatile elemental nitrogen (TVBN) content and pH during shrimp storage, highlighting the ability of the FE to monitor these variables as indicators of deterioration effectively. Initially, the fresh shrimp exhibited a TVBN value of 17.05 ± 0.29 mg/100 g and a pH of 6.52 ± 0.12. During storage at 25 °C, a gradual increase in protein degradation was observed in the first 12 h, reflected by the rise in TVBN. These results are consistent with the expected behavior of perishable foods, where proteolytic activity increases over time, as well-documented by Sen [ 55 ]. However, it is essential to note that the TVBN values in high-quality fish meat should remain between 5 mg/100 g and 20 mg/100 g, respectively. Fig. 5 Total volatile basic nitrogen content and pH in shrimp during storage at 25 °C. Different letters ( a ,  b ,  c ,  d ) indicate significant statistical differences at different storage times according to the Tukey test

Between 12 and 24 h of storage, the TVBN value in the shrimp showed a sharp increase, rising from 22.15 mg/100 g and a pH of 7.25 to 37.46 mg/100 g and a pH of 9.46. These data indicate an acceleration of protein degradation, which can be attributed to the action of proteolytic enzymes and microbial activity, both of which intensify as storage time increases. Moreover, TVBN values exceeding 35 mg/100 g are considered the critical limit for fish consumption safety Schormuller e Fette [ 56 ]. In this study, the TVBN values exceeded this limit after 24 h of storage, indicating that the shrimp had reached an unacceptable deterioration for human consumption (Fig.  6 ). Fig. 6 Changes in the population of Pseudomonas spp. during storage at 4 °C and 25 °C for shrimp samples coated with the control film (FC) and the active film (FE). Different lowercase letters (a, b, c, d) indicate significant differences among storage times within the same treatment ( p  < 0.05). Different uppercase letters (A, B, C, D) indicate significant differences among treatments at the same storage time ( p  < 0.05), according to Tukey’s multiple comparison test

These results reinforce the importance of continuous monitoring of food quality, particularly for highly perishable products like shrimp. They also demonstrate the potential of FE as effective colorimetric sensors to indicate when a product becomes unfit for consumption, allowing for real-time evaluation of shrimp freshness.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study demonstrated the great potential of films based on orange peel pectin, enriched with anthocyanin extract from purple sweet potato, as an innovative and effective solution for developing active and intelligent packaging. The resulting films exhibited enhanced physical and mechanical properties, such as increased tensile strength, flexibility, and thermal stability but also stood out due to the integration of bioactive compounds from the extract, which interacted efficiently with the pectin matrix. This combination resulted in more cohesive films with remarkable functional properties.

Moreover, the films’ notable antioxidant capacity represents a significant benefit for preserving foods sensitive to oxidation, suggesting a great potential for extending the shelf life of these products. The use of these films as freshness indicators was validated during the monitoring of shrimp deterioration, with the film showing a visible and sensitive response to pH changes and the release of volatile nitrogen compounds, both associated with product degradation.

Adding bioactive compounds, biodegradability, and using agro-industrial waste as raw material also provide additional sustainability to this technology, positioning these films as a promising and environmentally friendly alternative. Therefore, the combination of these properties makes pectin-based films enriched with anthocyanins a viable and promising option for creating intelligent packaging, offering benefits for both the food industry and environmental impact reduction.
